patterns.name: Two pointers
patterns.cue: Sorted array or string, comparing items from both ends, or two positions moving through it together.

template.ts:
let left = 0
let right = arr.length - 1
while (left < right) {
  if (isAnswer(arr[left], arr[right])) return [left, right]
  if (needBigger(arr[left], arr[right])) left++
  else right--
}

examples.title: Pair sum in a sorted array
examples.statement: Find two numbers in a sorted array that add up to a target.
examples.why: Sorted order tells you which pointer to move.

examples.title: Valid palindrome
examples.statement: Check whether a string reads the same forwards and backwards, ignoring punctuation.
examples.why: Compare the two ends and move inwards.

examples.title: Container with most water
examples.statement: Choose two lines that, with the x-axis, hold the most water.
examples.why: Always move the shorter side: it is the only move that can help.

examples.title: Remove duplicates in place
examples.statement: Remove duplicates from a sorted array without extra space.
examples.why: A slow write pointer and a fast read pointer move the same way.

confusions.difference: If both pointers move the same way to mark a contiguous run you are measuring, it is a sliding window.
If the data is unsorted, a pair sum needs a hash map instead (or a sort first).

patterns.name: Sliding window
patterns.cue: The best, longest or shortest contiguous subarray or substring that satisfies a condition.
patterns.complexity: O(n) time: each index enters and leaves the window once

template.py:
left = 0
best = 0
for right in range(len(arr)):
    add(arr[right])
    while not valid():
        remove(arr[left])
        left += 1
    best = max(best, right - left + 1)

examples.title: Max sum of k consecutive items
examples.statement: Find the largest sum of any k consecutive numbers.
examples.why: Fixed window: subtract the item leaving, add the item entering.

examples.title: Longest substring without repeats
examples.statement: Find the longest substring with no repeated characters.
examples.why: Grow right; shrink left until the window has no repeats.

examples.title: Minimum window substring
examples.statement: Find the smallest substring containing every letter of another string.
examples.why: Grow until valid, then shrink while it stays valid.

examples.title: Longest run with at most k distinct
examples.statement: Find the longest substring with at most k distinct characters.
examples.why: A hash map of counts tells you when the window breaks the rule.

confusions.difference: If numbers can be negative, a window can't decide when to shrink. Counting subarrays with sum k needs prefix sums and a hash map.
A subsequence can skip items, which usually needs DP. A substring or subarray is contiguous: a window.

patterns.name: Fast and slow pointers
patterns.cue: A linked list, or a sequence driven by a 'next' function, where you need the middle, a cycle, or the k-th from the end.

template.ts:
let slow = head
let fast = head
while (fast && fast.next) {
  slow = slow.next
  fast = fast.next.next
  if (slow === fast) return true // a cycle
}
return false // fast ran off the end; slow is at the middle
template.py:
slow = fast = head
while fast and fast.next:
    slow = slow.next
    fast = fast.next.next
    if slow is fast:
        return True  # a cycle
return False  # fast ran off the end; slow is at the middle

examples.title: Linked list cycle
examples.statement: Decide whether a linked list loops back on itself.
examples.why: Fast laps slow if there is a loop.

examples.title: Middle of a linked list
examples.statement: Return the middle node in one pass.
examples.why: When fast reaches the end, slow is halfway.

examples.title: Happy number
examples.statement: Repeatedly replace a number by the sum of the squares of its digits; does it reach 1?
examples.why: The sequence either reaches 1 or cycles: detect the cycle.

examples.title: Remove the k-th node from the end
examples.statement: Delete the k-th node from the end of a list in one pass.
examples.why: Start one pointer k steps ahead, then move both together.

confusions.difference: A set of visited nodes also finds a cycle, but uses O(n) space. Fast and slow uses O(1).

patterns.name: Hash map lookup
patterns.cue: You need to answer 'have I seen this?' or 'how many of these?' in constant time.

examples.title: Two sum (unsorted)
examples.statement: Find two numbers in an unsorted array that add to a target.
examples.why: Look up each number's complement among those already seen.

examples.title: Group anagrams
examples.statement: Group words that are anagrams of each other.
examples.why: Map each word's sorted letters (or letter counts) to its group.

examples.title: First unique character
examples.statement: Find the first character that appears only once in a string.
examples.why: Count every character, then scan again.

examples.title: Contains duplicate
examples.statement: Does any value appear at least twice?
examples.why: A set answers 'seen before?' in O(1).

confusions.difference: On sorted data, two pointers solve pair sums in O(1) extra space.
If the question is about sums of ranges, store running totals, often in a hash map.

patterns.name: Prefix sums
patterns.cue: Many range-sum questions, or counting subarrays with a given sum, even when numbers are negative.
patterns.complexity: O(n) to build, then O(1) per range query

template.py:
# prefix[i] = sum of arr[0..i-1]
prefix = [0]
for x in arr:
    prefix.append(prefix[-1] + x)

def range_sum(i, j):  # arr[i..j]
    return prefix[j + 1] - prefix[i]

examples.title: Range sum queries
examples.statement: Answer many questions of the form 'sum of items i to j'.
examples.why: Precompute once; each query is a subtraction.

examples.title: Subarray sum equals k
examples.statement: Count subarrays that add up to k, where numbers may be negative.
examples.why: Count earlier prefix sums equal to current − k with a hash map.

examples.title: Product of array except self
examples.statement: For each index, the product of all other items, without division.
examples.why: Multiply a prefix product by a suffix product.

examples.title: Pivot index
examples.statement: Find the index where the sum to the left equals the sum to the right.
examples.why: Total minus prefix gives the right side instantly.

confusions.difference: With only non-negative numbers, a sliding window also finds sums. With negatives, use prefix sums.

patterns.name: Binary search
patterns.cue: Sorted data, or a yes-or-no question that flips exactly once as the input grows, so you can search for the answer.
patterns.complexity: O(log n) time, or O(n log M) when each check scans the input

examples.title: Search a sorted array
examples.statement: Return the index of a target in a sorted array.
examples.why: Each comparison halves the range.

examples.title: First bad version
examples.statement: Versions are good until some point, then all bad; find the first bad one.
examples.why: A yes/no that flips once: search for the boundary.

examples.title: Search a rotated sorted array
examples.statement: Find a target in a sorted array that has been rotated.
examples.why: One half is always sorted; decide which side to keep.

examples.title: Ship packages within D days
examples.statement: Find the smallest ship capacity that delivers everything in D days.
examples.why: Binary search on the answer; check each capacity in O(n).

confusions.difference: Two pointers walk a sorted array in O(n) looking at pairs. Binary search jumps to one position in O(log n).

patterns.name: Stack (including monotonic)
patterns.cue: The most recent unfinished thing matters: nesting, matching, undo, or the next greater or smaller item.
patterns.complexity: O(n): each item is pushed and popped at most once

template.py:
# Monotonic stack: next greater element to the right
result = [-1] * len(arr)
stack = []  # indexes waiting for an answer
for i, x in enumerate(arr):
    while stack and arr[stack[-1]] < x:
        result[stack.pop()] = x
    stack.append(i)

examples.title: Valid parentheses
examples.statement: Check that every bracket is closed in the right order.
examples.why: The most recent opener must close first.

examples.title: Daily temperatures
examples.statement: For each day, how many days until a warmer one?
examples.why: A monotonic stack holds days still waiting.

examples.title: Evaluate reverse Polish notation
examples.statement: Evaluate an expression like '3 4 + 2 *'.
examples.why: Push numbers; an operator pops its two operands.

examples.title: Largest rectangle in a histogram
examples.statement: Find the largest rectangle under a bar chart.
examples.why: A monotonic stack finds each bar's nearest smaller neighbours.

confusions.difference: If items should be handled in arrival order (oldest first), that is a queue, as in BFS.
'Next greater' looks at neighbours in order: a stack. 'k largest overall' ignores position: a heap.

patterns.name: Breadth-first search
patterns.cue: The fewest steps in an unweighted graph or grid, or processing something level by level.

examples.title: Level-order traversal
examples.statement: Return a binary tree's values level by level.
examples.why: A queue keeps each level together.

examples.title: Shortest path in a grid
examples.statement: Fewest moves from the top-left to the bottom-right of a grid with walls.
examples.why: Every move costs 1, so BFS finds the fewest.

examples.title: Word ladder
examples.statement: Fewest one-letter changes to turn one word into another.
examples.why: Words are nodes; one-letter changes are edges.

examples.title: Rotting oranges
examples.statement: Minutes until every orange is rotten, spreading to neighbours each minute.
examples.why: Multi-source BFS: every rotten orange starts in the queue.

confusions.difference: DFS explores fully but can find a long path first. For fewest steps, use BFS.
If edges have different weights, BFS is wrong: use Dijkstra with a heap.

patterns.name: Depth-first search
patterns.cue: Explore everything reachable, or follow one path all the way down: components, flood fill, reachability.
patterns.complexity: O(V + E) time, O(V) space (the stack or recursion)

examples.title: Number of islands
examples.statement: Count groups of connected land cells in a grid.
examples.why: Each DFS from unvisited land marks one island.

examples.title: Flood fill
examples.statement: Recolour the region connected to a starting pixel.
examples.why: Visit every same-coloured neighbour.

examples.title: Max area of an island
examples.statement: Find the size of the largest island.
examples.why: Each DFS returns the size of what it explored.

examples.title: Path exists
examples.statement: Is there any route from A to B?
examples.why: Explore from A until you hit B or run out.

confusions.difference: DFS answers 'is it reachable?' but not 'in how few steps?'. For that, use BFS.
Backtracking is DFS over choices that undoes each choice to try the next.

patterns.name: Recursion and backtracking
patterns.cue: Generate every combination, permutation or subset, or search for a valid arrangement by trying choices and undoing them.

template.py:
results = []
def choose(start, path):
    results.append(path[:])  # record this combination
    for i in range(start, len(items)):
        path.append(items[i])  # choose
        choose(i + 1, path)    # explore
        path.pop()             # un-choose
choose(0, [])

examples.title: Subsets
examples.statement: Return every subset of a set of numbers.
examples.why: At each item, include it or not, then undo.

examples.title: Permutations
examples.statement: Return every ordering of a list.
examples.why: Pick each unused item next, recurse, then put it back.

examples.title: Combination sum
examples.statement: List every combination of numbers that adds to a target.
examples.why: Choose, recurse with the reduced target, un-choose.

examples.title: N-queens
examples.statement: Place n queens on an n × n board so none attack each other.
examples.why: Place row by row; undo when a row has no safe square.

confusions.difference: If you only need to **count** the ways or find the best one, the subproblems usually overlap: use DP. Backtracking **lists** them all.
DFS visits each node once. Backtracking revisits states through different choice paths.

patterns.name: Heaps and top-k
patterns.cue: The k largest, smallest, closest or most frequent, or always process the smallest or most urgent item next.
patterns.complexity: O(n log k) time, O(k) space

examples.title: Kth largest element
examples.statement: Find the k-th largest number in an unsorted array.
examples.why: A min-heap of size k keeps the k largest; its root is the answer.

examples.title: Top k frequent words
examples.statement: Return the k most frequent words.
examples.why: Count with a hash map, then keep a heap of size k.

examples.title: Merge k sorted lists
examples.statement: Merge k sorted linked lists into one.
examples.why: A heap of the k current heads gives the next smallest.

examples.title: Median of a data stream
examples.statement: Report the median as numbers arrive.
examples.why: Two heaps: a max-heap of the lower half, a min-heap of the upper.

confusions.difference: 'Next greater to the right' depends on position: a monotonic stack. 'k largest overall' doesn't: a heap.
If the data is already sorted, the k-th item is just an index.

patterns.name: Intervals
patterns.cue: Ranges with a start and an end: overlapping, merging, inserting, or scheduling rooms.
patterns.complexity: O(n log n) to sort by start, then O(n)

examples.title: Merge intervals
examples.statement: Merge all overlapping intervals.
examples.why: Sort by start; each interval either extends the last one or starts a new one.

examples.title: Insert interval
examples.statement: Insert a new interval into a sorted, non-overlapping list.
examples.why: Copy the ones before, merge the overlaps, copy the rest.

examples.title: Meeting rooms
examples.statement: Can one person attend every meeting?
examples.why: Sort by start and check each against the previous end.

examples.title: Meeting rooms II
examples.statement: The fewest rooms needed for all meetings.
examples.why: A min-heap of end times tracks rooms in use.

confusions.difference: 'Remove the fewest intervals so none overlap' sorts by **end** and is greedy.
Counting simultaneous meetings needs a heap of end times on top of sorting.

patterns.name: Tree traversal
patterns.cue: A binary tree question you can answer by combining the answers for the left and right subtrees, or that needs a particular visit order.
patterns.complexity: O(n) time, O(h) space for the recursion

examples.title: Maximum depth
examples.statement: Find the number of levels in a binary tree.
examples.why: 1 + the larger of the two subtree depths.

examples.title: Validate a BST
examples.statement: Check the binary search tree property holds everywhere.
examples.why: Pass down the (low, high) bounds.

examples.title: Lowest common ancestor
examples.statement: Find the deepest node that has both p and q below it.
examples.why: The answer is where p and q are found in different subtrees.

examples.title: Kth smallest in a BST
examples.statement: Find the k-th smallest value in a BST.
examples.why: In-order visits a BST in sorted order.

confusions.difference: If the question is about levels, or the nearest leaf, BFS can stop early.
Trees have no cycles, so tree recursion needs no visited set. Graphs do.

patterns.name: Graph traversal
patterns.cue: Things connected by relationships (dependencies, friendships, routes): build a graph, then search it, order it or find paths.
patterns.complexity: O(V + E) to build and search; Dijkstra is O((V + E) log V)

template.py:
# Build an adjacency list, then search with a visited set
from collections import defaultdict
adj = defaultdict(list)
for a, b in edges:
    adj[a].append(b)
    adj[b].append(a)  # undirected

examples.title: Course schedule
examples.statement: Can you finish every course given its prerequisites? In what order?
examples.why: Topological sort; a leftover cycle means impossible.

examples.title: Number of provinces
examples.statement: How many groups of cities are connected directly or indirectly?
examples.why: Count connected components.

examples.title: Clone graph
examples.statement: Deep-copy a graph of nodes and neighbours.
examples.why: Traverse with a map from original to copy.

examples.title: Network delay time
examples.statement: How long until a signal reaches every node, given weighted travel times?
examples.why: Weighted shortest paths: Dijkstra with a heap.

confusions.difference: A tree is a graph with no cycles and one parent per node, so it needs no visited set.
BFS is one way to search a graph; the pattern here is spotting that the problem is a graph at all.

patterns.name: Dynamic programming
patterns.cue: Count the ways, or find the minimum or maximum, where choices carry forward and the same subproblems keep coming back.
patterns.complexity: Number of states × work per state

template.py:
dp = [0] * (n + 1)
dp[0] = base
for i in range(1, n + 1):
    dp[i] = best(...)  # answers for smaller states, e.g. dp[i - 1], dp[i - 2]
return dp[n]

examples.title: Climbing stairs
examples.statement: How many ways to climb n stairs taking 1 or 2 steps?
examples.why: ways(n) = ways(n − 1) + ways(n − 2).

examples.title: Coin change
examples.statement: The fewest coins that make an amount.
examples.why: dp[c] = 1 + min over coins of dp[c − coin].

examples.title: House robber
examples.statement: Rob houses along a street for the most money without robbing two neighbours.
examples.why: dp[i] = max(skip house i, rob it + dp[i − 2]).

examples.title: Edit distance
examples.statement: The fewest single-letter edits to turn one word into another.
examples.why: A 2D table over prefixes of both words.

confusions.difference: If a local choice can be wrong (coins 1, 3, 4 for amount 6), you need DP.
Listing every option is backtracking. Counting them, or finding the best, is usually DP.

patterns.name: Greedy
patterns.cue: A locally best choice is provably safe: sort by the right key, then take whatever fits.
patterns.complexity: Usually O(n log n) for the sort, then O(n)

examples.title: Non-overlapping intervals
examples.statement: Remove the fewest intervals so the rest don't overlap.
examples.why: Sort by end and keep each interval that starts after the last kept end.

examples.title: Jump game
examples.statement: Can you reach the last index, where each value is your maximum jump?
examples.why: Track the furthest reachable index in one pass.

examples.title: Best time to buy and sell stock
examples.statement: One buy, then one sell: the maximum profit.
examples.why: Track the lowest price so far; the best sale is today's price minus it.

examples.title: Assign cookies
examples.statement: Give cookies to as many children as possible, each needing a minimum size.
examples.why: Sort both; give each child the smallest cookie that fits.

confusions.difference: Greedy never revisits a choice. If you can find a counter-example where it fails, use DP.
Interval problems are often greedy after sorting, but merging is a different job.
